pos: n. (king of Zobah in Syria, the greatest of the northern adversaries David subdued, written also Hadarezer)
etymology: From Hebrew Hadad'ezer, Hadad is help, compounding the name of the Syrian storm-god Hadad with 'ezer, help. The Authorized Version spells the same man Hadarezer in 2 Samuel 10 and 1 Chronicles 18-19, an interchange of d and r common in Hebrew manuscripts. His name confesses a false god as his helper, and the narrative is the story of that help failing.
biblical_def: Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, is the most formidable enemy of David's middle reign and the hinge of the empire's northern expansion. He is introduced at the Euphrates: “David smote also Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates” (2Sa 8:3). The spoil was enormous — chariots, horsemen, footmen, and the shields of gold that Shishak would later carry out of Jerusalem. Hadadezer would not stay beaten. When the Ammonites shamed David's ambassadors and needed an ally, he hired out his armies, and after the first defeat he escalated: “Hadarezer sent, and brought out the Syrians that were beyond the river: and they came to Helam; and Shobach the captain of the host of Hadarezer went before them” (2Sa 10:16). The outcome broke the coalition for a generation: “when all the kings that were servants to Hadarezer saw that they were smitten before Israel, they made peace with Israel, and served them” (2Sa 10:19). Even in defeat he seeded a future judgment: Rezon, one of his own captains, “fled from his lord Hadadezer king of Zobah” (1Ki 11:23) and was raised up by God as an adversary to Solomon. The brass David took from Hadadezer's cities went into the vessels of the temple, so that a Syrian king's war-metal ended in the house of the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Hadadezer; in sacred history he is king of Zobah in Syria, twice defeated by David and stripped of his chariots and treasure.
webster_full: HADADEZER, n. Hadad is help; a king of Zobah, a Syrian kingdom north of Damascus.
He is called also Hadarezer, by the common interchange of the letters.
David smote him as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates.
He hired the Syrians beyond the river to the aid of the children of Ammon, and was again defeated.
The brass taken from his cities was employed in the vessels of the house of God.
scriptures: David smote also Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates.

And when all the kings that were servants to Hadarezer saw that they were smitten before Israel, they made peace with Israel, and served them. So the Syrians feared to help the children of Ammon any more.
And God stirred him up another adversary, Rezon the son of Eliadah, which fled from his lord Hadadezer king of Zobah:
Gen 14:9
With Chedorlaomer the king of Elam, and with Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this king. The principle to recover is that the LORD subdues the strongest of His people's enemies and turns their spoil to His own worship, and that a name confessing a false helper is a name that will be disappointed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Hadadezer is a Syrian king in the books of Samuel and nobody has contested him. What his reign sets against the modern reader is the theology buried in his name. Hadad is help: he was called after the storm-god of Syria, the great rider of the clouds, and he lost a thousand chariots and twenty thousand footmen in a single campaign to a shepherd who had once written, “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). The narrative is not merely military history; it is a contest of names.

The principle to recover is that God is not a rival deity in a pantheon but the only living God, and that every other help is an invention. Isaiah puts the taunt at its sharpest: “he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god” (Isa 44:17). And the end of the story is the most pointed detail in it: the brass of Hadadezer's cities was carried to Jerusalem and made into vessels for the sanctuary. What Syria dedicated to Hadad, the LORD requisitioned for Himself.

pos: n. (the king of Egypt who sheltered Jeroboam and afterward, in the fifth year of Rehoboam, plundered Jerusalem and carried away the golden shields of Solomon)
etymology: From Hebrew Shiyshaq, rendering an Egyptian royal name; the first pharaoh in Scripture called by a personal name rather than the bare title Pharaoh. Egypt's own monuments record a campaign into Palestine by a king of this name, a corroboration of the sacred record, never its warrant.
biblical_def: Shishak enters the record as a refuge for a rebel: when Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam, “Jeroboam arose, and fled into Egypt, unto Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon” (1Ki 11:40). Five years after the kingdom split he came for the treasure. “And it came to pass in the fifth year of king Rehoboam, that Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem” (1Ki 14:25), and “he took away the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king's house; he even took away all: and he took away all the shields of gold which Solomon had made” (1Ki 14:26). The Chronicler supplies the reason the book of Kings leaves implicit: he came up “because they had transgressed against the LORD” (2Ch 12:2), and Shemaiah the prophet stated it to the assembled princes: “Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak” (2Ch 12:5). Rehoboam and the princes humbled themselves, and the LORD granted a partial deliverance with a lesson attached: “Nevertheless they shall be his servants; that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries” (2Ch 12:8). Rehoboam replaced the plundered gold with brass, and the guard carried brass shields into the house of the LORD ever after — a standing memorial in cheap metal of what apostasy costs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Shishak; in sacred history he is the king of Egypt who spoiled the temple and palace in the fifth year of Rehoboam.
webster_full: SHISHAK, n. A king of Egypt in the days of Solomon and Rehoboam.
He gave asylum to Jeroboam the son of Nebat when he fled from Solomon.
In the fifth year of Rehoboam he came up against Jerusalem with a great host.
He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the shields of gold which Solomon had made.
Rehoboam made in their stead shields of brass, and committed them to the guard.
scriptures: Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam. And Jeroboam arose, and fled into Egypt, unto Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon.
And he took away the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king's house; he even took away all: and he took away all the shields of gold which Solomon had made.

Then came Shemaiah the prophet to Rehoboam, and to the princes of Judah, that were gathered together to Jerusalem because of Shishak, and said unto them, Thus saith the LORD, Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak.
Nevertheless they shall be his servants; that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries.
corruption_summary: The modern habit is to explain Shishak's campaign wholly by Egyptian imperial policy and to treat the Chronicler's theological reading as later piety laid over the event. Scripture gives both causes and subordinates the political one to the moral.
corruption_paragraphs: Because a pharaoh of this name left a monumental list of conquered towns, the campaign is often narrated as a straightforward reassertion of Egyptian power over a weakened Palestine, with the Chronicler's “because they had transgressed against the LORD” treated as devotional overlay by a post-exilic writer. That is the historical-critical instinct at its most routine, and it is a category error. Scripture does not deny that Shishak had his own reasons, his own ambitions and his own logistics; it asserts that God governs armies, and that this particular army arrived in this particular year because Judah had forsaken Him. Secondary causes are real; they are not ultimate.

The doctrine at stake is providence — that God ordains whatsoever comes to pass and works through the free actions of men who are answerable for them. The Assyrian is the rod of God's anger and is judged for the arrogance with which he swings (Isa 10:5-12); Joseph's brothers meant it for evil and God meant it for good (Gen 50:20). The lasting monument of the episode is not on a temple wall in Egypt but in Jerusalem, where the golden shields were replaced with brass. A nation that spends its inheritance on idolatry will keep the ceremony and lose the substance, and the guard will still march, carrying cheaper metal.

pos: n. (one of the two princes of Midian slain by the men of Ephraim at Gideon's victory, and the rock named after him)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Oreb, a raven — the carrion bird, and a fitting name for a prince of the host that had eaten Israel bare for seven years. Not to be confounded with Horeb, the mount of God, which is a wholly different word.
biblical_def: Oreb is named with Zeeb in the rout that followed Gideon's three hundred, and the two are always spoken of together. The Ephraimites took the fords of Jordan ahead of the fleeing host and caught the princes: “And they took two princes of the Midianites, Oreb and Zeeb; and they slew Oreb upon the rock Oreb, and Zeeb they slew at the winepress of Zeeb, and pursued Midian, and brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side Jordan” (Jdg 7:25). The place kept the name of the man who died there, as places did — the rock Oreb stood as a marker in the land, and the memory outlasted the kingdom. Gideon used the victory to quiet Ephraim's jealous complaint with a soft answer: “God hath delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb: and what was I able to do in comparison of you?” (Jdg 8:3). Centuries later Asaph prays the same names over a new coalition: “Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna” (Psa 83:11), and Isaiah promises Assyria's overthrow “according to the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb” (Isa 10:26). A dead Midianite chief became a permanent figure of speech for what God does to the enemies of His people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Oreb; in sacred history he is a prince of Midian slain by the Ephraimites, and the rock upon which he fell.
webster_full: OREB, n. A raven; a prince of the Midianites in the days of Gideon.
He was taken at the passages of Jordan by the men of Ephraim and slain upon a rock.
The rock retained his name, and is called the rock Oreb.
His head and the head of Zeeb were brought to Gideon beyond Jordan.
The psalmist and the prophet Isaiah both allude to the slaughter at the rock of Oreb.

Jdg 8:3

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that Scripture keeps the memory of God's judgments as a ground of prayer, and that the church may plead old deliverances for present danger.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Oreb is a slain Midianite prince and nobody has contested him. What the rock Oreb sets against the modern habit of mind is the biblical use of memory. Asaph, facing a confederacy of ten nations, does not begin with strategy or with sentiment; he names a rock where God broke an army four hundred years earlier and asks Him to do it again. That is not nostalgia. It is the ordinary logic of covenant prayer: the God who acted is the God who is, and His past acts are the warrant for present petition.

The principle to recover is that the Christian remembers on purpose. Israel was commanded to set up stones and tell children what they meant; the Supper is kept “this do in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24); the psalms rehearse the Red Sea in every generation. A church with no memory prays small prayers, because it has nothing to plead but the present. Oreb is a hard name and the deliverance was a bloody one, but Isaiah reaches for it when he wants to promise a frightened people that Assyria will fall too.

pos: n. (the second of the two princes of Midian slain in the pursuit after Gideon's victory, killed at the winepress that afterward bore his name)
etymology: From Hebrew Ze'eb, a wolf. He and Oreb, the raven, are named for the two scavengers of the Hebrew world — the bird that follows an army and the beast that takes the flock — and the Midianite occupation they led is described in Judges as exactly that kind of predation.
biblical_def: Zeeb is inseparable from Oreb in the record: two princes of the Midianite host, taken by the men of Ephraim at the fords of Jordan while Gideon pressed the pursuit beyond the river. “they slew Oreb upon the rock Oreb, and Zeeb they slew at the winepress of Zeeb” (Jdg 7:25). The detail of the winepress is not decoration. The book of Judges opened Gideon's story with the young man who “threshed wheat by the winepress, to hide it from the Midianites” (Jdg 6:11) — an Israelite forced to do his threshing in a sunken vat, out of sight of the raiders who came up every harvest “as grasshoppers for multitude” (Jdg 6:5). The judgment came round to the same kind of place: a Midianite prince died in a winepress in the land his people had stripped. Ephraim brought the two heads to Gideon and then quarrelled with him for not calling them sooner, and his answer disarmed them by handing them the glory: “God hath delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb” (Jdg 8:3). Asaph prays the names centuries later against a fresh confederacy (Psa 83:11), which is how a wolf-named raider from the days of the judges became a fixed term in the vocabulary of Israel's prayer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Zeeb; in sacred history he is a prince of Midian slain by the Ephraimites at a winepress which took his name.
webster_full: ZEEB, n. A wolf; a prince of the Midianites in the time of Gideon.
He was taken with Oreb at the passages of Jordan by the men of Ephraim.
He was slain at a winepress, which was thenceforth called the winepress of Zeeb.
His head was carried to Gideon on the other side of Jordan.
Asaph in the eighty-third psalm prays that the nobles of Israel's enemies may be made like Zeeb.

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that God repays oppression in kind and in the very places where His people were humiliated, and that the deliverance is His even when the sword is another man's.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Zeeb is a Midianite prince killed at a winepress and nobody has contested him. What the winepress sets against the modern reader is the exactness of divine retribution. Israel had been driven into caves and dens and sunken vats to hide their grain from these men; a prince of these men bled out in a vat. Scripture notices such symmetries and expects the reader to notice them: Haman on his own gallows, Adonibezek with his thumbs cut off, the pit digged and the digger fallen into it.

The principle to recover is that vengeance belongs to God and is exercised through means He appoints. “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19) is not a denial that judgment happens but a statement of who owns it, and the civil sword is expressly said to be God's minister, “a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4). Ephraim held the fords and struck the blow, and Gideon still said, God hath delivered them into your hands. Both halves of that sentence are true, and a doctrine that keeps only one of them ends either in fatalism or in vigilantism.

pos: n. (the officer whom Abimelech set as ruler of Shechem, who kept the city for him against the rising of Gaal the son of Ebed)
etymology: From Hebrew Zebul, dwelling or habitation, from zabal, to dwell or exalt — the same element that appears in Zebulun and in the name of the Philistine idol Baal-zebub as it was later pronounced. His name means a dwelling, and his whole part in the story is holding a city he did not own.
biblical_def: Zebul serves in the darkest chapter of Judges, the reign of Abimelech son of Jerubbaal, who murdered seventy of his brethren upon one stone to make himself king at Shechem. Zebul is his deputy, resident in the city while Abimelech dwelt elsewhere. The crisis comes when a demagogue arrives: “And Gaal the son of Ebed said, Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? is not he the son of Jerubbaal? and Zebul his officer?” (Jdg 9:28). The insult was calculated — Abimelech was half a Shechemite by his mother and Gaal appealed to blood. Zebul heard it: “And when Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled” (Jdg 9:30). He sent word to Abimelech privily, advised an ambush by night, and then in the morning played the man's own words back to him at the gate: art thou he that said, Who is Abimelech that we should serve him? go out now and fight. The revolt collapsed, and “Zebul thrust out Gaal and his brethren, that they should not dwell in Shechem” (Jdg 9:41). Zebul is competent, loyal, and entirely in the service of a fratricide; and the chapter ends with Shechem sown with salt and Abimelech killed by a millstone, God having rendered the wickedness of both parties upon their own heads.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Zebul; in sacred history he is the ruler of Shechem under Abimelech, who put down the rebellion of Gaal.
webster_full: ZEBUL, n. A dwelling, a habitation; the officer of Abimelech in the city of Shechem.

In the morning he taunted Gaal with his own boast, and bade him go out and fight.
He thrust out Gaal and his brethren, that they should not dwell in Shechem.

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that loyalty and competence are not virtues in themselves, and that a good servant of a wicked master is participating in the wickedness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Zebul is Abimelech's deputy and nobody has contested him. What his career sets against the modern reader is the moral neutrality we grant to skill. Zebul does everything an able administrator should do: he detects the sedition, reports accurately, proposes a sound plan, times it well, and executes it. Every one of those competencies is deployed to preserve the rule of a man who slaughtered his seventy brothers on a stone. The narrative offers no commendation and no rebuke; it simply lets the reader watch ability serve murder.

The principle to recover is that God judges the cause a man serves and not merely the diligence with which he serves it. The chapter states the verdict twice: “Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren” (Jdg 9:56), and the men of Shechem got theirs in the same stroke. This is the standing question for anyone employed by an institution whose ends are corrupt — the excellence of the work does not sanctify the work. Christ put the whole calculation in one question: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mar 8:36).

pos: n. (one of the three sons of Anak driven out of Hebron by Caleb; also the king of Geshur, father of Maachah and grandfather of Absalom)
etymology: From Hebrew Talmay, connected with telem, a furrow or ridge — hence furrowed, or by another account bold. Two men bear it: a giant of Hebron in Joshua's day and a Syrian king in David's, four centuries apart.
biblical_def: Talmai is first one of the terrors that made ten spies faint. Reporting on the south country they said, “they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were” (Num 13:22) — three named giants in a walled city, and the report that followed sent a generation into the wilderness. Forty-five years later the same three names come up again, and this time the record is short: “And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak” (Jos 15:14). What terrified the ten, the one who wholly followed the LORD went and took at eighty-five. The second Talmai is king of Geshur, a small Aramean state east of the sea of Chinnereth. David married his daughter: Absalom was born of “Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur” (2Sa 3:3) — one of the political marriages that Scripture records without approving. When Absalom murdered Amnon he fled to his grandfather: “But Absalom fled, and went to Talmai, the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur” (2Sa 13:37), and stayed three years in a pagan court while his father mourned. The foreign alliance sheltered the murderer it had helped to produce.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Talmai; in sacred history it is the name of a son of Anak at Hebron, and of a king of Geshur whose daughter David married.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Talmai is a giant in one book and a Syrian king in another, and nobody has contested either. What the first Talmai sets against the reader is the difference faith makes to the same set of facts. The ten spies and Caleb saw identical men in an identical city. The ten concluded, “we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Num 13:33); Caleb concluded, “Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it” (Num 13:30). Unbelief is not a shortage of information. It is a judgment about God formed while looking at the same wall.

The second Talmai teaches the other half. David took a wife out of Geshur, a pagan house, and the son of that marriage murdered his brother and then had somewhere to run — three years of asylum in a court that owed the LORD nothing, followed by a rebellion that nearly cost David his throne. Scripture's prohibition of unequal alliance is not ceremonial fussiness; it is a warning about what comes home. “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2Co 6:14) is the New Testament's form of the same law, and the household of David is the standing case study.

pos: n. (the king of Elam who headed the confederacy of four kings that sacked Sodom and carried Lot away, and whom Abram overthrew with three hundred and eighteen trained servants)
etymology: From Hebrew Kedorla'omer, an Elamite name generally analysed as servant of Lagamar, an Elamite deity. He is the first named overlord in Scripture and the first man in the Bible to receive tribute from other kings.
biblical_def: Chedorlaomer king of Elam is the head of the first war narrated in the Bible. Four eastern kings held the cities of the plain in vassalage: “Twelve years they served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled” (Gen 14:4). His punitive campaign in the fourteenth year is described as a sweep down the whole eastern side of the Jordan rift, smiting Rephaims, Zuzims, Emims and Horites before turning back to the five rebel cities. The lineup is stated formally: “With Chedorlaomer the king of Elam, and with Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five” (Gen 14:9). Sodom and Gomorrah fell, the slime pits swallowed the fleeing armies, and the raiders took the goods and the people — including Lot. Then a private man with a household militia overtook an imperial coalition: Abram armed his trained servants, three hundred and eighteen of them, pursued to Dan, divided himself against them by night, and brought back all the goods and all the people. Melchizedek met him returning “from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that were with him” (Gen 14:17), and blessed him from the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth. The whole later theology of tithe and priesthood in Hebrews 7 hangs on that meeting, and the meeting happened because Chedorlaomer took the wrong nephew.

corruption_summary: Genesis 14 is routinely treated as a late legendary insertion because it names kings the modern historian cannot securely identify. The chapter reads as sober annals, and the dictionary receives it as history, not as saga.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard academic handling of this chapter is to call it an isolated fragment of uncertain date, its four kings unidentifiable and its details therefore suspect — legendary material shaped to glorify Abram. That verdict rests on an assumption, not a finding: that a narrative naming kings we cannot yet cross-reference is thereby doubtful. Genesis 14 is written in the manner of a campaign record. It gives regnal arithmetic, a route, the peoples smitten at each stage, the tactics of the pursuit, the size of Abram's force to the man, and the terms of the settlement afterward. Silence in the surviving tablets of the second millennium is not evidence; the record of that world is fragmentary in the extreme, and it has repeatedly filled in later.

The dictionary receives Moses' account as what it presents itself to be. The New Testament rests real doctrine on the chapter's historicity: Hebrews argues the superiority of Christ's priesthood from Melchizedek meeting a real Abraham returning from a real slaughter of real kings, and paying him a real tenth — “unto whom even the patriarch Abraham gave the tenth of the spoils” (Heb 7:4). Dissolve Chedorlaomer into legend and the argument of Hebrews 7 has nothing under it. That is the ordinary pattern: the historical-critical solvent is never applied to the history alone.

pos: n. (the father of Balak king of Moab, named repeatedly in the account of Balaam as the patronymic by which Balak is known)
etymology: From Hebrew Tsippor, a bird or sparrow, the same word used for the birds of the sacrifices and for the two birds of the leper's cleansing. The feminine form Tsipporah is the name of Moses' wife.
biblical_def: Zippor appears in Scripture only as a father. Every mention is in the formula Balak the son of Zippor, and it is used seven times across Numbers, Joshua and Judges. “And Balak the son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites” (Num 22:2) opens the whole Balaam narrative; “Balak the son of Zippor was king of the Moabites at that time” (Num 22:4) fixes the date; Balaam reports the summons as coming from “Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab” (Num 22:10); and when the prophet is compelled to bless instead of curse, he addresses the king by the same title: “Rise up, Balak, and hear; hearken unto me, thou son of Zippor” (Num 23:18). Nothing else is told of the man — not his reign, not his deeds, not his death. What the repeated patronymic accomplishes is a kind of witness: the writer will not let the king be a mere title. Balak is somebody's son, a link in a house, a Moabite of a particular family, standing on the plains of Moab hiring a prophet to curse the seed of Abraham. Centuries later Jephthah throws the name at the Ammonites as a settled precedent: “And now art thou any thing better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? did he ever strive against Israel, or did he ever fight against them,” (Jdg 11:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Zippor; in sacred history he is the father of Balak king of Moab, named only in that relation.

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that Scripture names fathers because men are not autonomous individuals but sons, standing in houses and under covenants they did not invent.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Zippor is a patronymic and nobody has contested him. What the formula sets against the modern mind is its assumption of the unattached self. Scripture almost never lets a man stand alone: he is the son of somebody, of a house, of a tribe, and his acts are recorded as the acts of that house. Balak is not simply a king with a policy toward Israel; he is Zippor's son, and Moab's treatment of Israel is entered against Moab for generations — which is exactly the logic of the statute barring Moab from the congregation because they hired Balaam (Deu 23:3-4).

The principle to recover is covenantal solidarity, which the modern doctrine of the free individual cannot accommodate and which the Bible assumes on every page. All die in Adam because they are in Adam; all in Christ are made alive because they are in Him: “For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” (1Co 15:22). The genealogies, the patronymics, the promises to a thousand generations of them that love Him — these are not primitive collectivism. They are the structure of the covenant, and a Christianity that cannot say the son of Zippor will also struggle to say in Adam and in Christ.

pos: n. (the woman of the valley of Sorek whom Samson loved, who sold the secret of his strength to the lords of the Philistines)
etymology: From Hebrew Delilah, most naturally taken from dalal, to be weak, brought low, to languish — hence she that weakened or the feeble one. The narrative uses the cognate idea at the crisis: his strength went from him, and he became weak as another man.
biblical_def: Delilah is the last of the three Philistine women in Samson's life and the only one Scripture says he loved: “he loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah” (Jdg 16:4). The lords of the Philistines bought her outright, eleven hundred pieces of silver from each of five cities, and her question was never disguised: “Tell me, I pray thee, wherein thy great strength lieth, and wherewith thou mightest be bound to afflict thee” (Jdg 16:6). Three times he lied, three times she bound him and cried that the Philistines were upon him, and three times he woke and broke the bonds — and stayed. The narrative is merciless about the mechanism: “when she pressed him daily with her words, and urged him, so that his soul was vexed unto death” (Jdg 16:16), and he told her all his heart. Then “she made him sleep upon her knees; and she called for a man, and she caused him to shave off the seven locks of his head; and she began to afflict him, and his strength went from him” (Jdg 16:19). The dreadful sentence is that he awoke and did not know “that the LORD was departed from him” (Jdg 16:20). The Philistines took him, put out his eyes, bound him with fetters of brass, and set him grinding in the prison house (Jdg 16:21). Delilah collects her silver and leaves the story; Scripture never mentions her again.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Delilah; in sacred history she is the woman of the valley of Sorek who betrayed Samson to the lords of the Philistines.
webster_full: DELILAH, n. A proper name; a woman of the valley of Sorek, beloved by Samson.

She pressed him daily with her words until his soul was vexed unto death, and he told her all his heart.
She caused the seven locks of his head to be shaven, and delivered him to his enemies.

And she made him sleep upon her knees; and she called for a man, and she caused him to shave off the seven locks of his head; and she began to afflict him, and his strength went from him.

corruption_summary: Delilah is now regularly rehabilitated as a woman of an occupied people acting rationally under pressure, and Samson recast as her abuser. The text presents a bought betrayer and a Nazarite who threw away his vow, and it holds each of them responsible.
corruption_paragraphs: The revisionist reading is by now the standard one in popular retellings: Delilah was a Philistine under a foreign strongman's attentions, with no power and no options, and the money was survival rather than greed; the real culprit is Samson, and the older reading of the passage is merely the suspicion of women dressed up as exegesis. Judges gives no support to any of it. The silver is offered before she acts and she does not decline it; she asks her question openly, four times, after three demonstrations that the answer will be used to bind him; she summons the barber; she cries the Philistines be upon thee while the ambush waits in the chamber. The text does not describe a cornered woman. It describes a paid one.

Nor does Scripture spare Samson, and this is why the chapter is not a tract against women but against a particular folly. He was a Nazarite from the womb who had already given away every part of the vow but the hair — he had touched the dead lion, drunk at a feast, and gone repeatedly to Philistine women — and the shaving was the last item on a long inventory of contempt. Proverbs describes the pattern exactly: “With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him” (Pro 7:21), and warns the young man to keep his way far from her door. The horror of Judges 16 is not the shears; it is the sentence, he wist not that the LORD was departed from him. A man may lose the presence of God by inches and be the last to notice.

pos: n. (the Agagite, father of Haman the enemy of the Jews, named in every formal mention of his son)
etymology: A Persian name taken into Hebrew as Hammedatha, generally explained as given by the moon or double. The Authorized Version attaches the Agagite to the family, marking descent from the royal house of Amalek and so setting the whole book of Esther inside an ancient quarrel.
biblical_def: Hammedatha is named five times in Esther and never apart from his son. The formula is heavy and deliberate: “did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him” (Est 3:1); “the king took his ring from his hand, and gave it unto Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the Jews' enemy” (Est 3:10); Esther pleads to reverse “the letters devised by Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite” (Est 8:5); and the record of the deliverance recites it once more: “Because Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had devised against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur, that is, the lot, to consume them” (Est 9:24). The point of the repetition is the second title, not the first. Agagite reaches back to Agag king of Amalek, whom Saul spared in disobedience and Samuel hewed in pieces before the LORD in Gilgal (1Sa 15:33), and behind Agag to the LORD's oath of perpetual war with Amalek for waylaying Israel in the wilderness. Mordecai is a Benjamite of the house of Kish — Saul's house. The gallows Haman built for the Jew, and the ten sons of Hammedatha's son who hung on it, close a war Saul left unfinished five hundred years earlier.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Hammedatha; in sacred history he is the Agagite, father of Haman the enemy of the Jews in the book of Esther.

corruption_summary: Esther is widely read as a secular court tale in which God does not appear and the Jews merely outmanoeuvre their enemies. The genealogy Scripture insists on — Agagite against Benjamite — makes the book a chapter of covenant history and its outcome the LORD's own oath being kept.
corruption_paragraphs: Because the divine name is absent from the Hebrew of Esther, the book is commonly handled as a nationalist novella or a festival legend with no theology in it, and the repeated patronymic is passed over as courtly formality. That is to miss what the writer is doing with a phrase he repeats five times. Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite sets the villain in the line of Amalek, of whom the LORD swore, “the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation” (Exo 17:16). Against him stands a man of the tribe of Benjamin descended from Kish. The reader is being told that this is not a palace intrigue but the last engagement of an ancient war.

That is also the answer to the alleged absence of God. Providence is the doctrine the book is written to display: nothing supernatural occurs, and every step — a deposed queen, a sleepless night, a forgotten record read aloud, a lot cast that fell almost a year away and gave time for a deliverance — is ordinary, and every step is governed. “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33) is the verse the Pur was designed to illustrate. Hammedatha's son cast lots against the covenant people and the God he did not name chose the date.
